title: The role of urban forestry in the air quality of capital cities
seoTitle: Urban forestry and air quality in capital cities
subtitle: Plant cover acts as a biological filter that reduces atmospheric pollution and protects public health in metropolises.
excerpt: Discover how the presence of trees in large cities alters air circulation and reduces the concentration of harmful atmospheric pollutants.
author: Daniele Morais
contentHtml:
The presence of trees in major Brazilian capital cities goes far beyond landscaping aesthetics, functioning as an indispensable living infrastructure for the purification of the atmosphere. The disorderly expansion of urban centers has drastically increased the emission of pollutant gases and particulate matter, making vegetation the primary natural element for mitigating these damages in the built landscape.

How plants filter the urban atmosphere

The physical and biological mechanism of air purification by trees is based on the interception of solid particles and the absorption of toxic gases generated by the burning of fossil fuels. Tree leaves have textured surfaces, covered by epicuticular waxes and trichomes, which act as microscopic traps for dust, soot, and suspended aerosols in the atmosphere. When wind blows through a tree canopy, the airflow is slowed down, forcing the deposition of these particles onto the foliage.

In addition to mechanical retention on the leaf surface, trees absorb pollutant gases through stomata, which are microscopic openings in the leaf epidermis essential for respiration and photosynthesis. Gases such as sulfur dioxide, carbon monoxide, and nitrogen oxides enter these pores and are metabolized by plant tissues, being transformed into less toxic compounds or stored in ways that do not harm the environment. This continuous process reduces the concentration of these pollutants at ground level, precisely where pedestrians circulate and where human exposure is most intense and direct.

Another determining factor in improving air quality is the thermal regulation exerted by vegetation. Trees mitigate urban heat islands by shading paved surfaces and through evapotranspiration, a process in which water is released into the atmosphere in the form of vapor. Cooling the air alters the dispersion dynamics of pollutants, reducing photochemical reactions that give rise to tropospheric ozone, a gas highly irritating to the human respiratory system that forms when intense solar radiation interacts with gases emitted by motor vehicles.

The historical evolution of greenery in metropolises

Concern for vegetation in Brazilian cities underwent profound transformations over the centuries, accompanying demographic growth and the industrialization process. In the early colonial and imperial periods, tree planting in urban areas primarily responded to hygienist criteria or aristocratic ornamentation, inspired by European models of tree-lined avenues and public promenades. Squares and parks were conceived as aesthetic refuges, without a deep technical understanding of the ecological role that vegetation would play in retaining atmospheric pollutants.

With the acceleration of the urbanization process in the mid-twentieth century, Brazilian capital cities suffered aggressive population densification, accompanied by the proliferation of the motor vehicle fleet and the installation of industries within urban perimeters. Narrow streets and tree-lined squares gave way to asphalted avenues and vertical buildings, creating true concrete canyons that hindered the natural circulation of winds. In this scenario of progressive environmental degradation, urban forestry ceased to be a mere ornament and transformed into an elementary sanitary requirement in the management of metropolises.

Municipal administrations began to incorporate arboricultural planning into road expansion and urban zoning projects, although often in a fragmented manner and without adequate botanical criteria. The choice of species began to be debated by agronomists, forestry engineers, and urban planners, who sought to balance the resistance of plants to urban pollution with the safety of underground and aerial infrastructure networks. This accumulation of technical knowledge consolidated urban forestry as an indispensable tool of urban environmental engineering, aimed directly at protecting public health and the ecological re-balancing of inhabited centers.

Pollution dynamics and species selection

The success of urban forestry in air purification depends directly on the correct choice of plant species and the spatial configuration of planting on public roads. Not all trees possess the same capacity to filter pollutants or tolerate the hostile environment of large metropolises, marked by compacted soils, restricted space for roots, and a high incidence of toxic gases. Species with dense canopies, evergreen leaves, and large leaf surface areas tend to be more efficient at retaining particulate matter than those that lose all their leaves during winter.

The spatial arrangement of trees on streets also determines the behavior of airflow and the dispersion of pollutants emitted by road traffic. In continuously tree-lined streets, canopies can act both as barriers preventing the rapid dispersion of gases to upper layers of the atmosphere and as efficient filters retaining pollution before it reaches the windows of residential buildings. Modern planning requires microclimatic studies to define planting density, avoiding the creation of stagnant corridors where exhaust gases become trapped at street level.

In addition to filtering capacity, species selection must consider the emission of biogenic volatile organic compounds by certain trees. Certain plants release substances that, when reacting with nitrogen oxides present in polluted atmosphere, can contribute to ozone formation in the lower troposphere. Therefore, municipal nurseries and planning departments prioritize native species that exhibit low photochemical reactivity, high resistance to urban pests, and deep root systems that do not damage sidewalks and underground water and sewage pipes.

Direct impacts on respiratory and cardiovascular health

Atmospheric pollution in capital cities represents one of the greatest risk factors for the development and worsening of chronic diseases, relentlessly affecting the respiratory and circulatory systems of the urban population. Fine particulate matter, composed of microscopic fragments of soot, ash, and metallic compounds, penetrates deeply into the airways during breathing, bypassing the natural filters of the nose and trachea until reaching the pulmonary alveoli. From there, these toxic particles manage to cross the blood-gas barrier and enter the bloodstream, triggering systemic inflammatory processes.

The presence of consolidated tree canopies near heavy traffic routes significantly reduces the concentration of these pollutants in the air inhaled by pedestrians, cyclists, and local residents. This plant barrier mitigates the incidence of asthma attacks, chronic bronchitis, allergic rhinitis, and acute respiratory infections, especially in children and the elderly, who constitute the most vulnerable age groups to the degradation of air quality. The reduction of the pollutant load in the air also exerts a protective effect on the cardiovascular system, reducing the incidence of heart attacks, strokes, and arterial hypertension associated with chronic exposure to toxic gases and soot.

The benefit of urban forestry also extends to the mental health and psychological well-being of capital city inhabitants, factors that are directly related to overall physical health. Visual and physical exposure to green environments reduces cortisol levels, lowers heart rate, and mitigates chronic stress generated by the fast pace of urban life and traffic noise. This state of physiological relaxation strengthens the immune system, creating a virtuous cycle in which green infrastructure acts simultaneously as an air purifier and a promoter of overall quality of life.

Myths and misconceptions about urban greenery

The relationship between urban vegetation and air quality is surrounded by myths that frequently misguide public policies and residents' perception of the role of trees. One of the most recurring misconceptions is the belief that urban trees are the main producers of the oxygen we breathe in cities. Although plant photosynthesis produces oxygen and absorbs carbon dioxide, most of the planet's atmospheric oxygen is generated by phytoplankton in the oceans. A tree's primary value in the city is not large-scale oxygen production, but rather the mechanical filtration of pollutants and the regulation of the microclimate.

Another common error is to assume that any tree planted in any location will bring immediate and indisputable environmental benefits. Inappropriate planting of invasive exotic species or trees incompatible with available space can cause severe structural disturbances, such as lifting sidewalks, disrupting power lines, and clogging storm drains during heavy rains. Poorly selected or weakened trees due to lack of maintenance can suffer branch drop or toppling, putting population safety at high risk and generating high repair costs for the public administration.

There is also the false idea that street trees increase air pollution by trapping traffic gases and preventing their dispersion. Although dense and poorly planned plant barriers can, in very specific situations of narrow urban canyons, accumulate pollutants near the ground, scientific studies demonstrate that the net benefits of urban forestry vastly outweigh the risks of stagnant retention. When spacing and pruning are performed with technical rigor, trees function as efficient dispersers and filters, consistently improving air quality compared to fully paved and vegetation-devoid streets.

Daily life transformed by the presence of trees

For the resident of a major capital, walking along tree-lined streets noticeably alters the daily experience in public space, providing a thermally more comfortable environment protected against exhaust smoke. The microclimate generated by canopy shade reduces the apparent air temperature by several degrees during the hottest days of the year, decreasing the need for intensive use of air conditioning systems in homes and workplaces, which generates an indirect electricity savings for society as a whole.

The urban landscape enriched with vegetation encourages the practice of outdoor physical activities, such as walking and running, which would be unfeasible or detrimental to health on public roads taken over by excessive heat and concentrated pollution. The reduction of dust and suspended particles allows the population to breathe cleaner air on their daily commute to work or school, decreasing work and school absenteeism caused by recurring respiratory diseases.

Furthermore, the presence of well-cared-for trees enhances residential and commercial property values, transforms the gray aesthetics of metropolises into more welcoming spaces, and fosters urban biodiversity, attracting birds and beneficial insects for local ecological balance. Citizens who understand and value urban forestry act as active supervisors in preserving the green heritage of their neighborhoods, demanding adequate maintenance, technical pruning, and the planting of new saplings in vegetation-deprived areas from public agencies.

Frequently asked questions about urban forestry and air quality

Are all tree species efficient at cleaning urban air? No. Efficiency varies considerably according to leaf anatomy, canopy density, and plant resistance to pollution. Species with rough, waxy leaves retain more particulate matter, while sensitive plants can die quickly when exposed to high concentrations of toxic gases on major avenues.

Can trees worsen pollution on very narrow streets? In cases of road corridors heavily confined by tall buildings and excessive, dense forestry, a barrier to the rapid dispersion of gases can occur. Therefore, urban planning requires specific wind circulation studies to define the size and proper spacing of trees on each type of road.

Why does cutting down old trees harm the local atmosphere so much? Large trees possess a leaf surface and root system incomparably larger than those of young saplings. Removing an adult specimen eliminates a highly potent biological filter that would take decades to be replaced by new plantings at the same proportion of environmental gain.

How can citizens help expand greenery on their street? Residents can request the planting of suitable saplings from competent municipal agencies, respecting technical guidelines for spacing and electrical wiring. Furthermore, protecting newly planted trees against vandalism and providing irrigation during dry periods ensures the survival of urban vegetation.

The future of breathing in Brazilian metropolises

The integration between urban planning and environmental preservation defines the level of habitability of Brazilian capital cities for coming decades. With the advancement of global climate change and the continuous densification of metropolitan areas, the expansion and technical management of urban forestry cease to be a landscaping choice and consolidate themselves as a central strategy for survival and public health.

Investing in botanical diversification, the protection of ecological corridors, and the rigorous maintenance of existing arboreal heritage ensures that cities continue to fulfill their function of housing the population without compromising the air quality essential to life. The future of major metropolises depends on the capacity to transform concrete into functional ecosystems, where technology and nature work together to purify the atmosphere we all breathe.
